teaser: A state inspector admired it, then ruled it too indecent to show. She was 27.
review_notes:
The photo shows a small bronze cast from one side, with the woman's back toward the camera; identification of which head and hand belong to which dancer is read from this angle and should be checked.
Armand Dayot's 1892 report (praise, objection to the nudity and closeness of the bodies, request for drapery, later recommendation of a marble that was never commissioned): standard account, wording paraphrased, not quoted.
Debussy keeping a cast of The Waltz in his study until his death: commonly reported, please confirm.
Eugène Blot's reduced bronze editions from 1905: please confirm date; the cast in the photo is assumed to be one of the small editions (about 46 cm / 18 in).
Catalog year 1893 corresponds to the first exhibition of the plaster; the composition was conceived from 1889.

lesson.text: In 1892 an inspector from the French Ministry of Fine Arts climbed the stairs to a young sculptor's studio in Paris to judge a plaster of two dancers. His report praised its force and skill. Then it said no. The couple were naked and pressed too close together, and such a work could not be placed in a public building.

The sculptor was Camille Claudel, twenty-seven years old. The inspector, Armand Dayot, suggested she dress her dancers. She spent months reworking the group and came back with what you see: bare torsos above, and below the waist a torrent of drapery that has nothing to do with decency. Dayot was won over and recommended an order for a marble. The order never came.

The first version is lost, so the revision is the only Waltz we know. And the cloth she was forced to add became the boldest thing in it. To see why, forget the bodies for a moment and consider the outline of the whole group against the wall.
Three lines show how far this couple has left the vertical.

lines.label: The lean
lines.text: From the two heads down to the far corner of the base, the group runs along one long slant. Nothing in it stands upright.

lines.label: The edge of the base
lines.text: This line rises from the left edge of the base. Both heads and the woman's whole back hang outside it, over empty air.

lines.label: The wave
lines.text: The drapery pours away from her hips in ridges that swing down to the right and spread over the base, like the wake behind a boat.

lesson.text: Real dancers in that position would fall. Sculpted ones should topple too, since bronze is heavy and the heads are far off center. The drapery is what saves them. It is a hidden buttress that carries the weight down to the base, and to the eye it reads as the swirl of the turn itself. Claudel turned a censor's demand into an engineering solution.
The Waltz is built on imbalance. Claudel sculpted the instant when two people can only stay upright because they are holding each other.
The composer Claude Debussy, a friend of Claudel in these years, owned a cast of The Waltz. He is said to have kept it in his study for the rest of his life.

When she modeled it, Claudel had spent nearly ten years in the studio of Auguste Rodin as his assistant, collaborator and lover. She was pulling away from him, and determined to be seen as more than his pupil. Rodin's couples kiss or grapple. Hers do something quieter, which you find by following their hands.

lesson.title: Where they touch
lesson.text: Seen from this side, the woman has her back to us. Follow the points of contact from top to bottom.

spots.title: Two heads
spots.text: His head bends down over her shoulder while hers sinks against him. The faces are barely defined. What counts is the tilt, heavy and trusting, like sleep.

spots.title: The hand at her waist
spots.text: His arm circles her bare back and the hand rests at her waist with the fingers loose. He steadies her without gripping.

spots.title: The joined hands
spots.text: On the other side an arm reaches out into space toward the clasped hands, the classic waltz hold. It points the opposite way from the lean and acts as a counterweight.

spots.title: Her name
spots.text: On the front of the base, cut into the metal, you can make out the signature: C. Claudel.

lesson.text: The surfaces differ on purpose. Skin is polished and catches the light in broad highlights. The drapery is torn and ridged like bark or seaweed, closer to something that grew than to cloth. That plant-like flow links the work to Art Nouveau, the style of curling natural lines that swept Europe in the 1890s.

The plaster was shown in Paris in 1893 and admired, but without a state order it could not be carved large. The Waltz survived because a dealer, Eugène Blot, cast it in bronze in small sizes from 1905, to stand on a mantelpiece or a piano. The cast in this photo is one of those, under half a meter tall (about 18 inches).

In 1913 Claudel's family had her committed to a psychiatric hospital. She remained confined for thirty years, until her death in 1943, and never sculpted again. Before her internment she had smashed many of her own plasters.

For decades she was a footnote in books about Rodin. That has changed. Since 2017 a museum devoted to her has stood in Nogent-sur-Seine, the town where she first modeled clay as a girl. Several versions of The Waltz are among the works shown there, still mid-turn and still about to fall.

quiz.question: Why did the state inspector first refuse The Waltz?
options: The nude dancers were pressed too close together
quiz.explanation: He admired the work but judged the nudity and closeness of the couple unfit for a public building.

quiz.question: What did Claudel add in response?
options: A sweep of drapery below the waist
quiz.explanation: She reworked the group with flowing drapery from the woman's hips.

quiz.question: What practical job does the drapery do?
options: It supports the leaning figures and carries their weight to the base
quiz.explanation: It works as a hidden buttress for a group that would otherwise topple.

quiz.question: How did The Waltz reach collectors?
options: As a huge marble in a Paris square
As small bronze casts made by the dealer Eugène Blot
As plaster copies sold by the state
quiz.explanation: The state marble was never ordered; Blot cast it in small bronzes from 1905.

quiz.question: Which composer owned a cast of the sculpture?
quiz.explanation: Debussy, a friend of Claudel, is said to have kept it in his study.

facts.text: The French state ordered a large marble version of The Waltz.
facts.explanation: The inspector recommended one, but the order never came.

facts.text: In this sculpture, both heads hang out beyond the edge of the base.
facts.explanation: The couple lean so far that their heads are over empty air.

facts.text: Camille Claudel spent the last thirty years of her life confined in a psychiatric hospital.
facts.explanation: She was committed in 1913 and died there in 1943.
